raw_case_text: A 68-years-old Hispanic man with chronic depression and anxiety, complained of night sweats, low grade fewer, and unexplained weight loss over 3 months. He had also 3 months of difficulty managing finances and keeping track of appointments. Abdominal tomography showed multiple intra-abdominal adenopathy and biopsy confirmed classic Hodgkin's lymphoma, of nodular sclerotic variety. He commenced treatment with ABVD chemotherapy (adriamycin, vinblastine, bleomycin, and dacarbazine). Six months after first presentation of the cognitive problems, he had acute onset of disorientation, inattention, psychomotor agitation, confusion, delusional ideas of grandiosity, auditory hallucinations, and alterations of anterograde memory. His score was 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) suggesting severe cognitive impairment. Two days later, the patient developed multiple episodes of psychomotor agitation and was unresponsive to a combination of neuroleptics and benzodiazepines. These neuropsychiatric changes were not attributed to the ongoing stable treatment with ABVD chemotherapy. Brain MRI showed a small established cerebellar infarction. Electroencephalogram was normal. Tests for metabolic encephalopathies were negative: complete blood cell count, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, liver function tests, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, antinuclear antibody, C-reactive protein, thyroid-stimulating hormone, antithyroglobulin, antithyroperoxidase antibodies, cortisol, vitamin B12, and laboratory tests for toxicology. Human immunodeficiency virus and rapid plasma reagin were negative. One oligoclonal IgG bands was found in the CSF, which was not observed in corresponding serum, but cell count and proteins were normal. CSF Gram stain and culture were negative. Extensive testing for infectious encephalitis was unremarkable (CSF PCR for E. coli K1, H. influenzae, L. monocytogenes, N. meningitidis, S. agalactiae, S. pneumoniae, Cytomegalovirus, Enterovirus, Herpes simplex 1 and 2, Herpes 6, Parechovirus, Varicella zoster, and Cryptococcus neoformans). The patient fulfilled the diagnostic criteria by Gultekin et al. for paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (PLE) and methylprednisolone one gram daily for 5 days was given. The patient recovered rapidly, with progressive improvement in memory and psychomotor agitation. CSF testing for commercially available neural and non-neural autoantibodies was negative (including against the N-Methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor, AMPA (alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) receptor, and VGKC (voltage-gated potassium channel complex). No informative autoantibodies were detected in the CSF paraneoplastic evaluation. AGNA-1 [Anti-Glial Nuclear antibody (Ab)], Amphiphysin Ab, ANNA-1, 2 and 3 (antineuronal nuclear Ab), CRMP-5-IgG (Collapsin response-mediator protein-5), PCA-1, 2, and 3 (Purkinje Cell Cytoplasmic Ab). Further testing of CSF for antibodies to metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (mGluR5) was positive on cell based assay and immunohistochemistry. This CSF sample was drawn before starting systemic steroids. At 30-days follow-up, the patient evolved oriented, attentive, without psychomotor agitation. MoCA was 30/30. He remains amnesic with respect to the hospitalization period, but with conservation of other memory modalities. Follow-up CT scan and EEG were unremarkable.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 68-year-old Hispanic man undergoing ABVD chemotherapy for classical Hodgkin lymphoma presented with acute disorientation, psychomotor agitation, grandiose delusions, auditory hallucinations, and anterograde amnesia on a 6-month background of cognitive decline.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Six months prior to the acute neuropsychiatric episode, the patient developed 3 months of night sweats, low-grade fever, unexplained weight loss, and difficulty managing finances and appointments, leading to a diagnosis of classical nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma and initiation of ABVD chemotherapy. Three months into stable chemotherapy (6 months after cognitive symptom onset), he developed acute disorientation, inattention, severe psychomotor agitation refractory to neuroleptics and benzodiazepines, grandiose delusions, auditory hallucinations, and anterograde memory loss.
subjective.past_medical_history: Classical nodular sclerosis Hodgkin lymphoma on ABVD chemotherapy; chronic depression and anxiety.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for night sweats, low-grade fever, weight loss, cognitive impairment, disorientation, agitation, delusions, and auditory hallucinations. Home medications included ABVD chemotherapy (doxorubicin, vinblastine, bleomycin, dacarbazine).

objective.physical_examination: Disoriented, inattentive, with severe psychomotor agitation, grandiose delusions, auditory hallucinations, and anterograde memory impairment, scoring 20/30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA).
objective.routine_investigations: CBC, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, LFTs, ESR, CRP, ANA, TSH, anti-thyroglobulin, anti-TPO, cortisol, vitamin B12, toxicology screen, HIV, and RPR were all normal or negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain MRI showed a small chronic cerebellar infarct; EEG was normal. Lumbar puncture CSF showed normal cell count and protein, 1 CSF-restricted oligoclonal IgG band, negative Gram stain and culture, negative CSF multiplex PCR panel (including Cryptococcus neoformans, HSV-1/2, HHV-6, VZV, CMV, enterovirus, parechovirus, and bacterial pathogens), negative standard commercial neural/onconeuronal autoantibodies (NMDA-R, AMPA-R, VGKC, AGNA-1, Amphiphysin, ANNA-1/2/3, CRMP-5, PCA-1/2/3), and positive CSF anti-metabotropic glutamate receptor 5 (anti-mGluR5) antibodies on cell-based assay and immunohistochemistry.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of anti-mGluR5 antibody-associated paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (Ophelia syndrome) secondary to classical Hodgkin lymphoma, confirmed by positive CSF anti-mGluR5 antibodies via cell-based assay and immunohistochemistry and fulfillment of Gultekin criteria after CSF PCR ruled out Cryptococcus neoformans and viral/bacterial meningoencephalitides. Treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 5 days) alongside ongoing ABVD chemotherapy, resulting in rapid neuropsychiatric recovery and a perfect MoCA score of 30/30 at 30-day follow-up.
